sessions.title: Public Choice Theory — Rent-Seeking & Regulatory Capture
sessions.description: Facilitated seminar discussion, questions and answers. Readings are encouraged, not necessary. Cameras remain on; discussions follow the Chatham House Rule. Sessions are not recorded.
submissionQuestions: Before this session, many of you said government should regulate to prevent market concentration. Having now explored regulatory capture and rent-seeking, how confident are you in that view? Discuss.
Identify a real-world example of rent-seeking or regulatory capture. What are the consequences, and are there reforms or interventions that could reduce it?

sessions.title: Individualism & Capitalism
sessions.description: Facilitated seminar discussion, questions and answers. Readings are encouraged, not necessary. Cameras remain on; discussions follow the Chatham House Rule. Sessions are not recorded.
submissionQuestions: What makes a political or economic structure immoral — and is communism immoral by that standard? Maxim grounded capitalism's moral legitimacy in its prohibition of physical force and its respect for individual rights. Applying this framework: does a system become immoral simply by permitting or requiring the use of force against individuals, or does intent and outcome also matter? Is communism immoral in principle, in practice, or both — and does the distinction matter?

If reason is humanity's defining characteristic, does capitalism uniquely enable it — or could other systems claim to do the same? Maxim argued that force "paralyses" and "negates" rational thought, making capitalism the only system compatible with human nature. But could a defender of social democracy argue their system also protects reason while correcting for market failures that suppress independent thought — such as monopoly control over media or economic insecurity limiting risk-taking?

Can a fully voluntary society handle the problem of private threats and intimidation — or does it require something beyond police and courts? Fellows raised concerns that economic power and the threat of violence can distort voluntary exchange without any formal coercion taking place. Maxim's response pointed to the legal system as the remedy. Is that sufficient? At what point, if any, does private power become indistinguishable in effect from political force?

sessions.title: Market Mechanisms in Higher Education
sessions.description: Facilitated seminar discussion, questions and answers. Readings are encouraged, not necessary. Cameras remain on; discussions follow the Chatham House Rule. Sessions are not recorded.
submissionQuestions: It is very hard to start a university in Australia, New Zealand, the United States, and most other Western countries due to regulation, permitting, and other barriers. Should we make it easier to start new universities and allow them to compete with incumbents?
Are income-contingent loans the least-worst way to fund higher education? Is there a more market-based alternative that would be better? If so, why?

sessions.title: Industrial Policy: The Role of the Government in Steering Economic Activity
sessions.description: Facilitated seminar discussion, questions and answers. Readings are encouraged, not necessary. Cameras remain on; discussions follow the Chatham House Rule. Sessions are not recorded.
submissionQuestions: Bob stressed that, even under a new industrial policy agenda, price signals should generally be left untouched. Why are price signals so important, and what happens when governments suppress, distort, or override them?

What are the main government failures associated with industrial policy? In particular, how serious are the risks of poor information, political capture, rent-seeking, permanent protection, and governments backing the wrong firms or industries?

How can industrial policy be prevented from simply rewarding politically connected industries? Are transparency rules, sunset clauses, competitive processes, and independent review enough — or is political favouritism an unavoidable feature of industrial policy?

sessions.title: Where to for the centre-right - a quantitative approach to public opinion
sessions.description: Facilitated seminar discussion, questions and answers. Readings are encouraged, not necessary. Cameras remain on; discussions follow the Chatham House Rule. Sessions are not recorded.
submissionQuestions: Jill's polling showed the Coalition's traditional advantage on economic management and immigration has eroded or converged with Labor's in recent years. If a centre-right party can no longer rely on "ownership" of these issues, what should it try to own instead?

Jill highlighted a growing rift between the centre-right's traditional donor base and its electoral base. The migration debate — where business groups tend to favour higher migration for growth while centre-right voters increasingly want it lower — is one example of this rift; another is business involvement in the promotion of social issues. How should a centre-right party manage this tension between its business supporters and its voters?

sessions.title: Reforms for another Century of Plenty
sessions.description: Facilitated seminar discussion, questions and answers. Readings are encouraged, not necessary. Cameras remain on; discussions follow the Chatham House Rule. Sessions are not recorded.
submissionQuestions: Chris argues that environmentalists should in fact seek more growth, not less, to address environmental degradation and climate change. How does more growth actually help solve environmental problems, rather than worsen them?

Australia has faced a decade of weak productivity and disposable income growth relative to OECD peers. What do you see as the single most important reform to reverse this, and why has it proven politically difficult?

sessions.title: Entrepreneurship and Australian Prosperity
sessions.description: Facilitated seminar discussion, questions and answers. Readings are encouraged, not necessary. Cameras remain on; discussions follow the Chatham House Rule. Sessions are not recorded.
submissionQuestions: What role should the entrepreneur play in society, and what policies, laws, or programs should be removed or added to promote entrepreneurship — if it should be promoted at all?

sessions.title: Law and Liberty
sessions.description: Facilitated seminar discussion, questions and answers. Readings are encouraged, not necessary. Cameras remain on; discussions follow the Chatham House Rule. Sessions are not recorded.
submissionQuestions: The speaker argued "anarchy and liberty are not the same thing." Are there cases where more law actually produced more freedom, not less?

The speaker suggested most 18C disagreement isn't "free speech vs. racism" but a dispute about where the threshold for legal intervention should sit. Where would you draw that threshold, and what test would you use to justify it?

sessions.title: Immigration Policy in Australia
sessions.description: Facilitated seminar discussion, questions and answers. Readings are encouraged, not necessary. Cameras remain on; discussions follow the Chatham House Rule. Sessions are not recorded.
submissionQuestions: Leaving aside the issue of numbers, what goal(s) should Australia want to accomplish with its immigration policy?
If rural areas are having trouble finding workers, why are rural Aboriginal unemployment rates so high?
